mainTopic: Spoiled deposits and the guardian's duty, and whether בית דין lets a relative manage the property of a captive or absent owner
overview: The amud continues the case of a deposit of produce that has spoiled. The גמרא explains that spoiled oil and honey still have uses, so selling them makes sense. It shows that the 'remedy' of the חכמים in the ברייתא is about saving the jars. It then explains that רבי מאיר and those חכמים disagree over whether even a small loss matters. Next the גמרא brings רבן שמעון בן גמליאל from the משנה, who says to sell the produce because doing so is like returning a lost item. It records two opposing rulings on the הלכה and settles an apparent problem with רבי יוחנן's view. The גמרא asks whether this dispute also decides if בית דין lets a relative manage a captive's property, and concludes that the two questions rest on separate reasons. It then brings the dispute of רב and שמואל on a captive's property, a challenge from a ברייתא and רב ששת's ruling, and a ברייתא about three kinds of absent owners' property. The amud ends by asking why two of these kinds are called נטושים and רטושים, and the answer comes on the next amud.

steps.title: What are spoiled oil and honey good for?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what use spoiled oil and honey could have, since חכמים want them sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: For what are they fit?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a simple question. If the oil has gone foul and the honey has spoiled, who would buy them?
steps.deeperAnalysis: חכמים in the ברייתא say the guardian should sell the spoiled produce in בית דין. Selling only makes sense if the items still have some value. So the גמרא asks what that value is.

phrases.english: For what are they fit?
phrases.notes: 'They' means the spoiled oil and honey from the ברייתא being discussed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens this section by questioning the practical value of the spoiled goods.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What practical use spoiled oil and honey still have, so that selling them makes sense.

steps.title: Oil for tanners, honey for camel wounds
steps.stepSummary: Spoiled oil can still be used by tanners, and spoiled honey can treat sores on camels.
steps.simpleTranslation: Oil is fit for tanners. Honey is fit for the wound of camels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that spoiled items still have real uses. Tanners can use the oil, and the honey can treat camels' sores.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Spoiled food is no longer good for people, but it is not worthless. Since a buyer can still be found, selling it in בית דין is a sensible step.

phrases.english: Oil is fit for tanners,
honey, for the wound of camels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Spoiled oil is used by tanners and spoiled honey treats camel sores, so they still have value.

steps.title: What remedy do חכמים mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes חכמים, who say the guardian 'makes a remedy' and sells, and asks what that remedy is.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the חכמים say: He makes a remedy for them and sells them in בית דין. What remedy does he make for them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the words of חכמים from the ברייתא again so it can ask about them. It wants to know what 'making a remedy' means when the produce is already ruined.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The produce has already spoiled and cannot be fixed. So it is unclear what kind of 'תקנה' (remedy) the guardian could possibly make. This quote sets up רב אשי's answer in the next step.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the 'remedy' fixes the spoiled wine, oil or honey. It cannot be fixed. The next step shows the remedy is about something else.

phrases.english: And the Sages say:
he makes a remedy for them
and sells them in court.
What remedy does he make for them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the value of the goods to the meaning of 'remedy' in the words of חכמים.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What 'remedy' can be made for produce that is already spoiled.

steps.title: The remedy is for the jars
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains that the remedy is to save the jars.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: For the jars.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי says the 'remedy' is not for the produce. It protects the jars the produce is stored in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the spoiled contents stay in the jars, the jars themselves can be ruined. By selling the contents and emptying the jars, the guardian saves the owner's jars.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
For the jars.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The remedy protects the jars, not the already-spoiled produce.

steps.title: What exactly is the dispute?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבי מאיר and חכמים really disagree about.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It asks what the real point of disagreement is between רבי מאיר and חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר agrees that when produce is losing value faster than normal, the guardian should sell it. So the גמרא wants to locate the exact point where the two sides split.

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the remedy is known to be about the jars, the גמרא asks what principle divides the two views.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The underlying principle behind the dispute of רבי מאיר and חכמים.

steps.title: Big loss versus small loss
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר holds that חכמים cared only about a big loss. חכמים hold that they cared even about a small loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: One Sage holds: they were concerned about a large loss, but not about a small loss. And the other Sage holds: they were concerned even about a small loss.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the dispute. It is about whether a small loss, like ruined jars, is enough reason for the guardian to get involved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר says only a large loss justifies handling someone else's deposit. Losing the jars is small, so the guardian should not touch it. חכמים say even a small loss counts, so he should sell the contents and save the jars.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר: only a large loss matters, so leave the spoiled produce alone. חכמים: even a small loss (the jars) matters, so sell it.

phrases.english: For one master holds:
phrases.notes: This first master is רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: for a large loss, they were concerned;
for a small loss, they were not concerned.
And the other master holds:
even for a small loss they were also concerned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They disagree whether חכמים were concerned about a small loss such as damage to the jars.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets out a general principle: how big a loss must be before a guardian should act on someone else's property.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: sell it, like returning a lost item
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבן שמעון בן גמליאל from the משנה: the guardian sells it in court, since this is like returning a lost item.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: He should sell them in בית דין, because he is like one who returns a lost item to its owners.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the next opinion in the משנה, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. He says the guardian should sell the produce in בית דין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His reason is that saving the owner's money is like השבת אבידה (returning a lost item). Selling before more value is lost is a way of giving the owner back what he would otherwise lose.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא quoted in the משנה
One who returns a lost item

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
he should sell them in court,
because he is like one who returns a lost item to the owners.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the ברייתא and returns to the next opinion in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The guardian sells the produce in court, since protecting the owner's value is like returning a lost item.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the הלכה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא son of רבי יעקב reports in the name of רבי יוחנן that the הלכה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: רבי אבא son of רבי יעקב said in the name of רבי יוחנן: The הלכה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ruling about which opinion we follow. רבי יוחנן rules like רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now we only heard the different opinions. This step adds a practical ruling: the guardian should sell, as רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (introduces a statement of אמוראים)
A leading אמורא of ארץ ישראל

phrases.aramaic: אִתְּמַר, רַבִּי אַבָּא בְּרַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: It was stated: Rabbi Abba son of Rabbi Yaakov said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
The halacha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִתְּמַר, רַבִּי אַבָּא בְּרַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a practical ruling on the opinion just quoted in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

steps.title: רב נחמן: the הלכה follows חכמים
steps.stepSummary: רבא reports in the name of רב נחמן that the הלכה follows חכמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said in the name of רב נחמן: The הלכה follows the words of the חכמים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second, opposing ruling. רב נחמן rules like חכמים, not like רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now there are two reports that disagree about the practical law. These חכמים are the first opinion in the משנה, who say the guardian should not touch the produce at all. They are not the חכמים of the ברייתא in steps 3-6, who said to sell. So רבי יוחנן says to sell, like רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, while רב נחמן says to leave it alone.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two reports about the הלכה: רבי יוחנן rules like רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, and רב נחמן rules like חכמים.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume the last ruling quoted is automatically the final word. Here the גמרא simply records two opposing rulings.

phrases.english: And Rava said that Rav Nachman said:
The halacha follows the words of the Sages.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a ruling that opposes the one in step 8.

steps.title: Why did רבי יוחנן need to rule here at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי אבא's report. רבי יוחנן already gave a general rule that the הלכה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל in almost every משנה, so why would he need to say it again for this case?
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבי יוחנן already said this once! רבה בר בר חנה reported that רבי יוחנן said: Every place where רבן שמעון בן גמליאל taught something in our משנה, the הלכה follows him. There are only three exceptions: the guarantor, צידן, and the final evidence.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the report from Step 8. If רבי יוחנן already has a general rule covering this case, a special ruling here seems unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's general rule says the הלכה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל in every משנה except three cases. Our case is not one of the three, so it should already be covered. That makes רבי אבא's specific report look extra and pointless.

keyTerms.meaning: a guarantor (one who backs up a loan)

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא אַמְרַהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן חֲדָא זִמְנָא,
phrases.english: But didn't Rabbi Yochanan already say it one time?

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: As Rabba bar bar Chana said that Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל מָקוֹם שֶׁשָּׁנָה רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
phrases.english: Every place where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel taught
in our Mishnah, the halacha follows him,
except for the guarantor, and Tzaidan,
phrases.notes: These are short names for cases elsewhere in ש״ס: a guarantor on a loan (בבא בתרא), and something that happened in the town of צידן (גיטין).

phrases.english: and the final evidence.
phrases.notes: This is a case in סנהדרין about evidence brought late.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אַמְרַהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן חֲדָא זִמְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for רבי אבא's report of רבי יוחנן's ruling in Step 8
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבא's report that רבי יוחנן ruled like רבן שמעון בן גמליאל in this case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A general rule from רבי יוחנן already covers this case, so a specific ruling here is extra

steps.title: Two אמוראים report רבי יוחנן differently
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי אבא and רבה בר בר חנה disagree about what רבי יוחנן held.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are אמוראים who disagree about the view of רבי יוחנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The two reports come from two different אמוראים, and they don't agree on what רבי יוחנן said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה בר בר חנה says רבי יוחנן gave a general rule. רבי אבא holds there was no such general rule, so a specific ruling for this case was needed. Each report is consistent on its own terms.

phrases.english: They are amora'im who disagree
phrases.notes: The disagreement is between רבי אבא (Step 8) and רבה בר בר חנה (Step 10).

phrases.english: about the view of Rabbi Yochanan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 10
steps.terutzResolutionType: Dispute among transmitters (two אמוראים report the same master differently)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All reports of רבי יוחנן must fit together, so the specific ruling seems extra
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי אבא did not hold of a general rule, so for him the specific ruling was needed

steps.title: Linking our מחלוקת to a captive's property
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests our מחלוקת also decides another question: whether בית דין lets a relative take over and manage the property of a captive.
steps.simpleTranslation: From רבן שמעון בן גמליאל we learn that we let a relative take over a captive's property. From the חכמים we learn that we do not let a relative take over a captive's property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws an inference. It suggests that each side of our מחלוקת also takes a side on a related question about a captive's property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל lets the guardian act on the owner's behalf, like returning a lost item. So the same logic would let a relative manage a captive's land. The חכמים say not to touch another person's things, so they would also not let a relative step in.

keyTerms.meaning: we learn; it can be inferred
we bring down; we let someone take over and manage

phrases.english: From Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel we learn
that we bring down a relative into the property of a captive.
phrases.notes: "Bring down" means בית דין lets the relative take over the land and manage it.

phrases.english: From the Rabbis we learn
that we do not bring down a relative into the property of a captive.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new line, using the מחלוקת to decide a related case
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל would let a relative manage a captive's property; the חכמים would not

steps.title: The link is rejected: each side's reason may not apply there
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the link. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל may only allow acting here because the produce itself is being destroyed. The חכמים may only forbid it here because of רב כהנא's or רב נחמן בר יצחק's reasons, which don't apply to a captive's land.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do you know? Maybe רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said this here only because the produce itself is being destroyed. But there, he may agree that we do not let a relative take over. And maybe the חכמים said this here only because of רב כהנא's reason, or because of רב נחמן בר יצחק's reason. But there, they may agree that we do let a relative take over.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on Step 12. It shows that each side's reason in our case may be special to rotting produce, so we can't carry it over to a captive's property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With rotting produce, the item itself disappears. A field left alone stays whole, so רבן שמעון בן גמליאל might not allow stepping in there. The חכמים's reasons were that a person prefers his own produce, or that the owner may have set it aside as תרומה or מעשר. Those reasons don't apply to a captive's land, so the חכמים might allow a relative to manage it.

keyTerms.meaning: and from where (do you know this)?
he only said it here, not beyond
the principal (the item itself) is being destroyed

steps.whatToRemember: Our מחלוקת cannot prove anything about a captive's property. Each side's reason here may be special to rotting produce.
steps.confusionAlert: The sides flip here. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל might NOT allow a relative in, and the חכמים might allow it. The גמרא is only showing the opposite is possible, not deciding it.

phrases.english: And from where do you know this?

phrases.aramaic: דִּלְמָא עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל הָכָא,
phrases.english: Perhaps Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel only said it here
because the principal is being destroyed,
phrases.notes: The fruit itself is rotting away. A field, by contrast, stays whole even if nobody works it.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הָתָם הָכִי נָמֵי דְּאֵין מוֹרִידִין.
phrases.english: but there, indeed we do not bring down a relative.

phrases.aramaic: וְעַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמְרִי רַבָּנַן הָכָא,
phrases.english: And the Rabbis only said it here
either because of Rav Kahana's reason,
phrases.notes: This is his earlier reason: a person prefers his own produce.

phrases.english: or because of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's reason.
phrases.notes: This is his earlier worry: maybe the owner already set aside this produce as תרומה or מעשר for other produce.

phrases.english: But there, indeed we do bring down a relative.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִמַּאי? דִּלְמָא עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference of Step 12
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the full link between the produce case and the captive's property case, for both sides
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Each side's reasoning (destroyed principal; רב כהנא's or רב נחמן בר יצחק's reasons) may be specific to rotting produce and not apply to land

steps.title: Doesn't שמואל show the two rules share one reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the claim from step 13 that the two topics have separate reasons. שמואל rules like רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and also rules that a relative may manage a captive's property, which looks like one shared reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are you really saying these are two separate reasons? But רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: the הלכה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. And שמואל also said: בית דין lets a relative take over a captive's property. Isn't that because both rules come from one reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on its own answer from step 13. It points to שמואל, who holds both 'act' positions, as if one idea is behind both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 13 the גמרא said the two topics might be unrelated. Here it notices that שמואל rules 'yes, act' in both places: like רבן שמעון בן גמליאל in our case, and 'yes, send a relative' for the captive. That pattern suggests one shared reason, which would bring back the link the גמרא just rejected.

keyTerms.meaning: Is this to say...? (opens a challenge to what was just said)
Literally 'we bring down a relative': בית דין lets a relative step in and manage the land

phrases.english: Is this to say that they are two separate reasons?
But didn't Rav Yehuda say in the name of Shmuel:
The halacha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel,
and Shmuel also said:
We let a relative go down and manage a captive's property.
Isn't that because it is one reason behind both?

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמֵימְרָא דִּתְרֵי טַעְמֵי נִינְהוּ? וְהָאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rejection in step 13 that separated the two topics.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 13 that the two topics depend on different reasons.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שמואל holds 'act' in both cases, which suggests one shared reason connects them.

steps.title: No, שמואל has two separate reasons
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that שמואל's two rulings rest on two different reasons. It is just a coincidence that he says 'act' in both.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, they are two separate reasons.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends its earlier position. שמואל ruled each case on its own grounds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Agreeing on the outcome in two cases does not prove the same reason is behind both. שמואל can allow acting in our case because the produce is being ruined, and separately allow a relative into a captive's land for a different reason.

phrases.english: No, they are two separate reasons.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Separating the reasons: same outcome, different reasoning.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל ruling 'act' in both cases shows one reason links them.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל's two rulings are independent and happen to agree.

steps.title: רב נחמן proves the two rules are separate
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports the 'two reasons' view. רב נחמן rules like חכמים, who don't allow acting in our case, yet he still lets a relative manage a captive's property.
steps.simpleTranslation: This also makes sense, because רבא said in the name of רב נחמן: the הלכה follows חכמים. And רב נחמן also said: we let a relative take over a captive's property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings proof for its answer. One אמורא holds 'don't act' in our case but 'act' for the captive.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the two topics shared one reason, ruling like חכמים here would mean refusing to send a relative into a captive's land. רב נחמן rules like חכמים but still sends the relative. So his rulings can only make sense if the reasons are different.

keyTerms.meaning: So too it makes sense (introduces support)
Like the words of the חכמים

phrases.english: So too, it makes sense,
since Rava said in the name of Rav Nachman:
The halacha follows the Chachamim.
And Rav Nachman also said:
We let a relative go down and manage a captive's property.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי נָמֵי מִסְתַּבְּרָא, דְּאָמַר רָבָא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 15 with evidence.
steps.raayaObject: That the two topics depend on two separate reasons.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב נחמן's two rulings: like חכמים in our case, yet allowing a relative into a captive's property.

steps.title: Conclusion: two separate reasons
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws the conclusion from רב נחמן's rulings: the two topics rest on two separate reasons, and it confirms this.
steps.simpleTranslation: So learn from this that they are two separate reasons. Yes, learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes this back-and-forth. It confirms that our מחלוקת does not decide the captive question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'אלא' means: since רב נחמן's rulings would contradict each other otherwise, the only way out is two reasons. The repeated 'שמע מינה' is the גמרא's stamp of agreement.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather / so the only option is
Learn from it (draws and confirms a conclusion)

steps.whatToRemember: Our מחלוקת (whether to step in to save the ruined produce) does not decide whether בית דין sends a relative into a captive's land. Each question has its own reason, as רב נחמן's rulings show.

phrases.english: Rather, learn from it:
They are two separate reasons. Yes, learn from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ: תְּרֵי טַעְמֵי נִינְהוּ, שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the proof in step 16.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The two topics depend on two separate reasons, so our מחלוקת does not settle the captive question.

steps.title: רב and שמואל argue about a captive's property
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now quotes a separate dispute. רב says בית דין does not let a relative take over a captive's property, and שמואל says it does.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: about a person who was taken captive, רב said we do not let a relative take over his property, and שמואל said we do let a relative take over his property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic: an אמוראים dispute about the captive's property itself, now on its own and not tied to our משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the captive's property came up only as a possible link to our מחלוקת. Here the גמרא brings the actual argument: רב says no relative, שמואל says yes. This matches שמואל's ruling quoted in step 14.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (introduces an אמוראים dispute)
A person who was taken captive

phrases.english: It was stated:
A captive who was taken captive,

phrases.aramaic: רַב אָמַר: אֵין מוֹרִידִין קָרוֹב לִנְכָסָיו,
phrases.english: Rav said: We do not let a relative go down into his property.
Shmuel said: We do let a relative go down into his property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the link question to the captive dispute itself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: no relative is sent into a captive's property. שמואל: a relative is sent in.

steps.title: If we heard he died, everyone agrees
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא narrows the רב and שמואל dispute. If word came that the captive died, all agree a relative is sent in to manage the property.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where they heard that he died, everyone agrees that we let a relative take over.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא marks off one case that is not part of the argument. This sets up the next move, where it will explain which case they do argue about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dispute between רב and שמואל is now limited. When there is a report that the captive died, even רב agrees a relative goes in. So the real argument must be about a captive who is still believed alive or whose fate is unknown.

keyTerms.meaning: They heard about him (a report came)
Everyone agrees (literally: the whole world doesn't argue)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רב refuses in every case. Here the גמרא says even רב lets a relative in once there is a report of death. Their argument is only about other cases.

phrases.english: Where they heard about him that he died,
everyone agrees that we let a relative go down.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּשֶׁשָּׁמְעוּ בּוֹ שֶׁמֵּת כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the scope of the dispute stated in step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When there is a report that the captive died, all agree a relative is sent into his property.

steps.title: Where רב and שמואל really argue, and why
steps.stepSummary: The dispute is only when there is no report that the captive died. רב fears the relative will damage the land. שמואל says he will not, because he is paid like a sharecropper.
steps.simpleTranslation: They argue when no one heard that the captive died. רב says: we do not send a relative in, because he might ruin the property. שמואל says: we do send him in. Since the Master said we pay him like a sharecropper, he will not ruin it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes narrowing the רב and שמואל dispute. It tells us the exact case they argue about and each side's reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner may come back, the relative knows he will have to return the land. So he might farm it hard for quick profit and wear it out. That is רב's worry. שמואל answers that the relative is paid a sharecropper's share of the crops, so he wants the land to stay productive. That gives him a reason to care for it properly.

keyTerms.meaning: When they argue (this is the case they disagree about)
We 'send down,' meaning בית דין lets a relative take over the property
A sharecropper who works a field for a share of the crops

steps.whyThisMatters: Each side's reason is the key to everything that follows. The ברייתא brought next will be read as either supporting or not supporting רב's 'do not send down' position.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי פְּלִיגִי בְּשֶׁלֹּא שָׁמְעוּ בּוֹ שֶׁמֵּת.
phrases.english: When they disagree, it is where they did not hear that he died.
רב says: we do not send down (a relative),
lest he ruin them (the properties).
And שמואל says: we do send down,
since the Master said
we assess them like a sharecropper,
he will not ruin them.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי פְּלִיגִי בְּשֶׁלֹּא שָׁמְעוּ בּוֹ שֶׁמֵּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes step 19: after the case where all agree (word came that he died), it gives the case where they argue.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the captive is not reported dead, רב says no relative is sent in (fear of damage), and שמואל says one is sent in (sharecropper pay prevents damage).

steps.title: A ברייתא says the children may not go down to their father's property
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר learns from the extra words 'והיו נשיכם' that the wives cannot remarry and the children cannot go down to the father's property. This seems to contradict שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא. רבי אליעזר says: from 'My anger will burn and I will kill you,' I already know their wives will be widows and their children orphans. So why does the פסוק add 'and your wives will be widows'? It teaches that the wives will want to remarry and will not be allowed, and the children will want to go down to their father's property and will not be allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge שמואל, who lets a relative go down to a captive's property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra words of the פסוק teach a further punishment. The men vanish with no proof of death, so their families are stuck. The wives may not remarry, and the children may not go down to the property. That sounds exactly like רב's 'we do not send down,' so it attacks שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: Why does the פסוק need to say this?
To go down into (take over) the property

phrases.english: They raised an objection: רבי אליעזר says:
From the implication of what is said,
'My anger will burn and I will kill you,'
I know that their wives are widows
and their children orphans.
So why does the פסוק say
'And your wives will be (widows), etc.'?
phrases.notes: The 'etc.' stands for the rest of the פסוק: 'and your children orphans.'

phrases.english: It teaches that their wives will seek to remarry
and they will not allow them,
and their children will want to go down to their father's property
and they will not allow them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks שמואל's position from step 20 with a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that בית דין sends a relative down to a captive's property
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says בית דין does not let the children go down to a missing father's property, which matches רב and contradicts שמואל.

steps.title: רבא: the ברייתא only forbids going down to sell
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the ברייתא only blocks the children from taking the land as their own to sell. Managing it is still allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: we learned 'to go down and sell.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends שמואל by reading the ברייתא more narrowly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבא, 'going down' in the ברייתא means taking over as heirs, with the right to sell. That is forbidden because the father has not been proven dead. Simply managing the land for him, as שמואל allows, is a different thing and is not ruled out.

keyTerms.meaning: To go down and sell (take it as an inheritance)

phrases.english: רבא said: 'to go down and to sell' is what we learned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the meaning of the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא forbids any going down to the property, even just to manage it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא only forbids taking the property as an inheritance to sell. Managing it is allowed, so שמואל stands.

steps.title: רב ששת rules on a real case from the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: A case came up in נהרדעא, and רב ששת decided it from this ברייתא. He ruled that relatives may not go down to a captive's property.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a case in נהרדעא, and רב ששת decided it from this ברייתא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about a real case. It sets up a debate about how to read the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת used the ברייתא as proof that בית דין does not let a relative go down at all. That reads it like רב, not the way רבא did. This sets up the challenge that comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא (a teaching of the תנאים outside the משנה)

phrases.english: There was an incident in נהרדעא,
and רב ששת resolved it from this ברייתא.
phrases.notes: He ruled that the relatives may not go down to the captive's property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same ברייתא from step 21, but reads it as a full ban, against רבא's narrow reading in step 22.
steps.raayaObject: That בית דין does not send a relative down to a captive's property
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of רבי אליעזר on 'והיו נשיכם אלמנות'

steps.title: רב עמרם: maybe the ברייתא only means selling
steps.stepSummary: רב עמרם challenges רב ששת's proof. He suggests the ברייתא only forbids going down to sell, just as רבא said.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב עמרם said to him: perhaps we learned 'to go down and sell'?
steps.whatsHappening: רב עמרם questions רב ששת's ruling by raising the same narrow reading רבא gave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ברייתא only forbids selling, it proves nothing about simply managing the land. Then רב ששת's ruling has no source. This attacks the proof itself.

phrases.english: רב עמרם said to him:
Perhaps 'to go down and to sell' is what we learned?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב עַמְרָם: דִּלְמָא לֵירֵד וְלִמְכּוֹר תְּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב ששת's proof from step 23 using רבא's reading from step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's proof from the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא could mean only that the children may not go down to sell, so it does not ban managing the land.

steps.title: רב ששת: the children are like the wives, so it means not at all
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת mocks the far-fetched reading and proves his own. The children are taught alongside the wives. The wives may not remarry at all, so the children may not go down at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: perhaps you are from פומבדיתא, where they pass an elephant through the eye of a needle? The ברייתא teaches the children like the wives. Just as there it is not at all, here too it is not at all.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת rejects רב עמרם's narrow reading and defends his ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'elephant through a needle' remark means: that reading is a clever stretch. The ברייתא puts the wives and the children side by side. The wives get no permission at all, so the children also get no permission at all, not even to manage the land.

keyTerms.meaning: פומבדיתא, a city known for very sharp, sometimes overly clever reasoning
An elephant through the eye of a needle (a far-fetched argument)

steps.whatToRemember: רבא reads the ברייתא as only forbidding selling, which allows managing the land like שמואל. רב ששת insists that the children, like the wives, get nothing at all, which matches רב.
steps.confusionAlert: רב ששת's 'perhaps you are from פומבדיתא' is not a geography question. It is a sharp way of saying the reading is too far-fetched.

phrases.english: He said to him: perhaps you are from פומבדיתא,
where they pass an elephant through the eye of a needle.
But it teaches their children similar to their wives,
phrases.notes: Some versions don't have the word in square brackets; with it, the children are taught side by side with the wives.

phrases.english: just as there (the wives) it is not at all,
so too here (the children) it is not at all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב עמרם's challenge from step 24 and defends רב ששת's ruling from step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Proof from the parallel structure of the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא might only forbid selling the father's property.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because the children are taught together with the wives, who get no permission at all, the children may not go down to the property at all.

steps.title: Managing a captive's property is an old dispute
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא states that whether a relative may be put onto a captive's property is already a dispute between תנאים, and it gets ready to quote the ברייתא that shows it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whether we put a relative onto a captive's property is a dispute between תנאים, as a ברייתא teaches:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes a short claim: the argument we have been discussing already appears among the תנאים. This line sets up the ברייתא that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the question was argued through later rulings and readings of verses. Now the גמרא says the question is older. Earlier תנאים already disagreed about it, so each side of the later dispute has a תנא to lean on.

keyTerms.meaning: We put someone down onto the property, meaning בית דין lets him manage it
It is a dispute between תנאים
As it is taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: And whether we put a relative onto a captive's property
is a dispute of תנאים, as it is taught:

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמוֹרִידִין קָרוֹב לְנִכְסֵי שָׁבוּי תַּנָּאֵי הִיא, דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the back-and-forth over the ברייתא of 'והיו נשיכם', the גמרא shows the question was already argued by תנאים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whether a relative is put onto a captive's property is a dispute of תנאים.

steps.title: A relative on a captive's property is not removed
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that someone who goes onto נכסי שבויין is not removed. Even if he hears the owners are coming and quickly harvests and eats, he keeps the produce. It then defines נכסי שבויין.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone goes down to a captive's property, we do not take it away from him. Even if he heard the owners were on their way, and he hurried, picked the produce and ate it, he is a diligent person who earns his reward. What counts as captives' property? A case where his father, brother, or another relative he inherits from went overseas, and people heard that he died.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives its first case, the captive's property. The relative who manages it is protected, and the ברייתא explains which situation it means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The relative is allowed to stay on the land. He may even keep the crop he harvested just before the owners came back, as a reward for his work. The ברייתא then defines this category: the relative went overseas and people heard he died.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not take it out of his hands
They are on their way and about to arrive
Quick and diligent, so he earns the gain

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the three names in this ברייתא. Here 'captives' property' is the case where people heard the relative died. The next case, נטושים, is when nobody heard he died.

phrases.english: One who goes down to the property of a captive –
we do not take it out of his hands,
and not only that, but
even if he heard that they are on their way and coming,
phrases.notes: 'They' are the owners returning to their land.

phrases.english: and he got there first, picked and ate –
he is diligent and earns the gain.
And this is what captives' property is –
where his father or his brother
or one of the relatives he inherits from
went off overseas,
and people heard about him that he died.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַיּוֹרֵד לְנִכְסֵי שָׁבוּי – אֵין מוֹצִיאִין אוֹתוֹ מִיָּדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins quoting the ברייתא promised in step 26.
steps.raayaObject: That the question of going onto an absent person's property is discussed and argued about by תנאים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's first case, נכסי שבויין, where the relative is not removed.

steps.title: A relative on abandoned property is removed
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that someone who goes onto נכסי נטושים is removed. It defines this category as a relative who went overseas when nobody heard that he died.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone goes down to abandoned property, we take it away from him. What counts as abandoned property? A case where his father, brother, or another relative he inherits from went overseas, and nobody heard that he died.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives its second case, abandoned property. Here the relative is taken off the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only difference from the first case is that nobody heard the owner died. Because of that one detail, the תנא קמא does not let the relative stay. This is the point where רבן שמעון בן גמליאל will disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: Abandoned property, left behind by someone who went overseas and is not known to have died
We take it out of his hands

phrases.english: One who goes down to abandoned property –
we take it out of his hands.
And this is what abandoned property is:
where his father or his brother
or one of the relatives he inherits from
went off overseas
and people did not hear about him that he died.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַיּוֹרֵד לְנִכְסֵי נְטוּשִׁים – מוֹצִיאִין אוֹתוֹ מִיָּדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא with a second category that gets the opposite ruling.
steps.raayaObject: The view of the תנא קמא in the dispute: a relative is removed when the owner is not known to have died.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's ruling on נכסי נטושים.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: abandoned property is like captives' property
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says he received a tradition that נטושים are treated like שבויין, so the relative is not removed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said: I heard that abandoned property is like captives' property.
steps.whatsHappening: Here is the other side of the dispute between תנאים. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees with the ruling about abandoned property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא removes the relative from abandoned property. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says it gets the same rule as captives' property, so the relative may stay. This argument is the 'dispute of תנאים' that the גמרא promised in step 26.

keyTerms.meaning: I heard, meaning I have a tradition

steps.whatToRemember: Abandoned property (נטושים): the תנא קמא says the relative is removed, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says he stays, just like on captives' property.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives each side of the later argument about putting a relative onto a captive's property an earlier תנא to rely on.

phrases.english: And Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said:
I heard that abandoned property is like captives' property.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל: שָׁמַעְתִּי שֶׁהַנְּטוּשִׁים כִּשְׁבוּיִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view to the ruling on נטושים in step 28.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Abandoned property gets the rule of captives' property, so the relative is not removed.

steps.title: A relative on forsaken property is removed
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds a third category, נכסי רטושים: the relative was here, and nobody knows where he went. Someone who goes onto this property is removed.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone goes down to forsaken property, we take it away from him. What counts as forsaken property? A case where his father, brother, or another relative he inherits from was here, and he does not know where they went.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends with a third case, forsaken property. Here the relative is removed, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל does not argue about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this case the owner did not travel overseas to a known place. He was here and simply disappeared, and nobody knows where he went. With so little known about him, the relative is not allowed to stay on the land.

keyTerms.meaning: Forsaken property, left behind by someone who was here and vanished to an unknown place

phrases.english: One who goes down to forsaken property –
we take it out of his hands.
And this is what forsaken property is –
where his father or his brother
or one of the relatives he inherits from was here,
and he does not know where they went.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַיּוֹרֵד לְנִכְסֵי רְטוּשִׁים – מוֹצִיאִין אוֹתוֹ מִיָּדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא with a third category.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who goes onto forsaken property is removed.

steps.title: Why the names 'abandoned' and 'forsaken'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what makes one category 'נטושים' and the other 'רטושים'. What do the two names mean?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is special about these, that they are called 'abandoned', and what is special about those, that they are called 'forsaken'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to ask about the names of two categories in the ברייתא. This question sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נטושים and רטושים sound very similar. Both are cases of an owner who is gone and not known to have died. The גמרא wants to know what each name is based on and what it tells us about each case.

phrases.english: What is different about those, that they call them 'abandoned',
and what is different about these, that they call them 'forsaken'?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי שְׁנָא הָנָךְ דְּקָרוּ לְהוּ נְטוּשִׁים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the names of two categories from the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason behind the names נטושים and רטושים, and what each name tells us about its case.
